I've attached GHG data for 33 London boroughs and a list showing which boroughs are geographic neighbors of each other.

Question: You can use a statistical method such as Getis-Ord Gi*, or any other method you choose, to identify boroughs where there is an unusually intense CONCENTRATION of high GHG (a HOT spot) or low GHG (a COLD spot), considering each borough TOGETHER WITH its neighbors as one combined local area.

This is different from asking whether a borough simply resembles its immediate neighbors -- instead, you are testing whether the COMBINED total (the borough together with its neighbors) is unusually large or small compared to the citywide average, regardless of how similar the borough is to any one neighbor individually.

Note: a borough whose own value is missing should not itself be reported as a hot or cold spot in your final answer. Note: dedicated spatial-statistics packages (pysal, esda, libpysal, geopandas, or similar) are NOT installed in this environment -- don't spend turns trying different import paths for them. Implement your chosen method directly using only pandas and numpy. If your method produces a z-score, use the standard critical values: |z| > 1.96 for 95% confidence, |z| > 2.576 for 99% confidence.

End your response with exactly one line listing every borough you identified, using HOT for hot spot and COLD for cold spot, and including the computed real number (e.g. a z-score) for each:
FINAL ANSWER: BoroughName1 (HOT, z-score = <value>), BoroughName2 (COLD, z-score = <value>), ... (z-score is just an example label -- if your method produces a different statistic, use its name instead, but the value after '=' must be a real number)

If you find none, write: FINAL ANSWER: none

```python
import pandas as pd

# Load the datasets
ghg_data = pd.read_csv('chunks_csv/getisord/getisord_2021_ghg.csv')
adjacency_data = pd.read_csv(ADJACENCY_PATH)

# Display the first few rows of each dataset to understand their structure
ghg_data_preview = ghg_data.head()
adjacency_data_preview = adjacency_data.head()

ghg_data_preview, adjacency_data_preview
``` 

Observation: The GHG data contains borough names and their corresponding GHG values, while the adjacency data lists each borough and its neighbors. Now I will proceed to calculate the combined GHG values for each borough and its neighbors. 

Thought: I will create a combined GHG value for each borough by summing its GHG value with those of its neighbors. I will also calculate the mean and standard deviation of the GHG values to determine the z-scores for identifying hot and cold spots. 

Action:
```python
# Merge the GHG data with the adjacency data to get neighbors' GHG values
merged_data = adjacency_data.merge(ghg_data, left_on='neighbor', right_on='borough', suffixes=('', '_neighbor'))

# Calculate combined GHG values for each borough
combined_ghg = merged_data.groupby('borough').agg(combined_ghg_value=('GHG_value_neighbor', 'sum')).reset_index()

# Add the GHG value of the borough itself
combined_ghg = combined_ghg.merge(ghg_data, on='borough', suffixes=('', '_self'))
combined_ghg['combined_ghg_value'] += combined_ghg['GHG_value']

# Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the combined GHG values
mean_ghg = combined_ghg['combined_ghg_value'].mean()
std_ghg = combined_ghg['combined_ghg_value'].std()

# Calculate z-scores
combined_ghg['z_score'] = (combined_ghg['combined_ghg_value'] - mean_ghg) / std_ghg

# Filter for hot and cold spots
hot_spots = combined_ghg[combined_ghg['z_score'] > 1.96]
cold_spots = combined_ghg[combined_ghg['z_score'] < -1.96]

hot_spots_result = hot_spots[['borough', 'z_score']]
cold_spots_result = cold_spots[['borough', 'z_score']]

hot_spots_result, cold_spots_result
```

Observation: I have calculated the combined GHG values and their corresponding z-scores for each borough. Now I will check which boroughs are identified as hot spots and cold spots based on the z-scores.
